mcqs.question: A checkout page must respond within 300ms or users abandon. A log-ingestion pipeline must process 1M events/sec but no one checks per-event delay. What should govern each system's optimization?
options: Both systems should be optimized for throughput, since that's the universal performance metric
The checkout page should optimize for throughput; the pipeline should optimize for latency
Neither has enough information to decide — it depends only on the language used to build them
The checkout page should optimize for latency (its SLA is response time); the pipeline should optimize for throughput (its SLA is events/sec)
mcqs.explanation: The right metric follows the SLA that actually matters: a user waiting on a page cares about response time, while a pipeline with no one watching per-item delay cares about sustained volume. Neither system benefits from optimizing the metric no one is checking.

mcqs.question: Which of the following typically improves both latency and throughput at once, rather than trading one for the other?
options: Increasing the batch size on a write queue
Reusing a pool of warm database connections instead of opening a new one per request
Request coalescing across many concurrent identical calls
Adding an artificial delay to smooth out traffic spikes
mcqs.explanation: Connection pooling removes per-request handshake overhead, which lowers latency, while also letting the database serve more requests/sec without that overhead eating capacity — a genuine win on both axes. Batching, coalescing, and deliberate delay all trade latency for throughput (or the reverse) by design.

mcqs.question: Increasing the batch size on a write queue improves overall throughput. What's the most likely effect on p99 latency for individual writes?
options: p99 latency can increase, since some writes now wait for the batch to fill before being processed
p99 latency always decreases proportionally to the throughput gain
p99 latency is unaffected by batch size — only p50 changes
Batch size has no relationship to latency, only to server cost
mcqs.explanation: Larger batches mean a write can sit waiting for the batch to fill, which shows up worst in the tail — p99 specifically can spike even as average throughput rises. It isn't just a p50 effect, and the two metrics don't move in lockstep in the direction the other wrong options claim.

mcqs.question: A team doubles their queue's batch size and reports throughput went up 40%. What should they check before calling this a pure win?
options: Nothing further — a throughput increase is always an unambiguous improvement
Whether the server's CPU usage decreased as a result
Whether p99 latency for individual requests got worse as a side effect of the larger batch
Whether the database's disk usage changed
mcqs.explanation: Throughput and latency can move in opposite directions, so a throughput win needs to be checked against the tail latency it may have quietly cost — an average-only view would hide exactly this regression. CPU and disk usage aren't the axis this trade-off actually lives on.
